Life history data for the Smooth skate (Malacoraja senta) indicate that neonates emerge from their egg cases measuring approximately 31 cm [Lb = approximately 31 cm] in total length at birth. This species, a small-bodied skate endemic to the Northwest Atlantic, demonstrates a notably slow growth trajectory typical of many deepwater rajiforms. Field studies conducted in the Gulf of Maine and along the Scotian Shelf have provided estimates of several key demographic parameters. Under prevailing thermal conditions of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], the embryonic development period extends considerably; the age at birth has been calculated at approximately 1,460 days [ab = approximately 1,460 days], reflecting the protracted incubation phase associated with cold-water environments. This extended developmental duration is consistent with the reduced metabolic rates observed in other boreal elasmobranchs and likely imposes constraints on population recovery rates. Understanding these foundational life-history milestones is essential for parameterizing demographic models used in fisheries management, particularly given the species' vulnerability to bottom trawl bycatch and its limited intrinsic capacity for rapid population increase compared to more fecund teleost species.

The maximum reproductive rate of Malacoraja senta has been estimated under the cold conditions (4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]) that dominate its benthic habitat. The available data suggest that individual females can achieve a peak reproductive output of approximately one pup per litter [N_R_i = approximately one pup per litter], with a frequency of roughly 2 litters per year [F_R_i = roughly 2 litters per year] when conditions are favorable, yielding about 2 pups per year [Ri = about 2 pups per year]. This low fecundity is characteristic of many skate species and is compensated by the production of relatively large, well-yolked eggs that develop into fully formed juveniles at parturition. The maximum reproductive rate is intimately linked to the thermal regime, as colder temperatures slow both oocyte development and gestation. The documented rate highlights the species' conservative life-history strategy, which renders it particularly sensitive to elevated adult mortality from fishing activities. Comparative analyses with sympatric skates such as Amblyraja radiata suggest that Malacoraja senta occupies the slower end of the life-history continuum among Northwest Atlantic rajiforms.

Adult body size in Smooth skate exhibits moderate sexual dimorphism, with males attaining a smaller ultimate total length than females. Males achieve a maximum total length of approximately 88 cm [Li = approximately 88 cm], whereas females, which tend to grow more slowly but over a longer period, reach a substantially larger terminal size of about 70 cm [Li = about 70 cm]. This disparity in ultimate length is accompanied by corresponding differences in body mass; the ultimate wet weight for males has been estimated at roughly 7,000 grams [Wwi = roughly 7,000 grams], while females achieve a slightly lower asymptotic mass of around 3,400 grams [Wwi = around 3,400 grams] when considering the allometric relationship between length and weight derived from field specimens. These size differences likely reflect divergent selective pressures on the sexes, with larger body size in females conferring advantages in fecundity through increased abdominal cavity volume for egg production. The length-weight relationships follow a typical power-law function common among elasmobranchs and are consistent with values reported for other members of the family Rajidae.

The timing of sexual maturation in Smooth skate shows a subtle but discernible difference between the sexes. Puberty occurs when females reach approximately 54 cm [Lp = approximately 54 cm] in total length at puberty, whereas males attain sexual maturity at a slightly larger size of around 56 cm [Lp = around 56 cm] in total length at puberty for males. This pattern, in which males mature at a comparable or slightly greater length than females despite reaching a smaller ultimate size, has been documented in several other skate species and may reflect sex-specific energetic allocation strategies. The onset of gonadal activity in this species is thus closely tied to the attainment of a critical body size rather than a fixed chronological age, although the cold temperatures of the deep-sea environment impose a slow developmental pace. Field surveys indicate that individuals typically reach this threshold several years after parturition, passing through a prolonged juvenile phase during which they are particularly vulnerable to predation and fishing pressure.

Longevity records for Malacoraja senta indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5,110 days [am = approximately 5,110 days] under the cold thermal conditions of the Northwest Atlantic shelf (4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]). This lifespan, equivalent to roughly 14 years, positions the Smooth skate as a relatively long-lived species within the rajiform community, though not as extreme as some deepwater chondrichthyans that can exceed several decades. The extended lifespan is coupled with a late age at first reproduction and low fecundity, forming a classic K-selected life-history syndrome that limits the species' capacity to withstand high levels of anthropogenic mortality. Growth increments in vertebral centra, analyzed from museum collections, reveal a slow but steady increase in body length throughout life, with asymptotic size being reached only in the oldest individuals. The ecological implications of this extended lifespan include a slow population turnover rate and a prolonged reproductive window, during which individual females may produce multiple pups across successive breeding seasons, partially offsetting the low per-event fecundity characteristic of the species.
